head.title: Vegan Catering Dubai | Menus & Prices | myCHEF
head.meta_description: Vegan catering in Dubai from AED 700pp — plant-based mains and grazing boards and more, with vetted chefs and full service. Bespoke menus for any event. Get a quote.
head.h1: Vegan Catering in Dubai — Real Prices, Menus and Timings

opening_paragraph: myCHEF arranges vegan catering in Dubai from AED 700 per person — a fully plant-based spread built by a vetted chef who designs the menu, cooks on site, serves and clears up. You give us the date, guest count and venue; during our published business hours your itemised quote arrives promptly, with no deposit needed to see the numbers or the menu directions.

replace_in_block.new_heading: What does vegan catering in Dubai include?
new_paragraphs: Vegan catering services in Dubai cover the whole meal from design to takedown, so you host instead of plate boxes of salad. Your booking includes a tailored menu and tasting, a vetted chef and their team, on-site cooking or delivery, the service, and the cleanup afterwards. As the team coordinating your booking, we cost the food, the labour and any rentals in one itemised quote, with allergens flagged and every dish confirmed free of meat, dairy, eggs and honey. Nut-conscious, gluten-free and soy-free vegan menus may be available on request, subject to confirmation by the assigned culinary partner, and we scale the same vegan food catering from an intimate dozen to several hundred guests. Nothing on the quote is a hidden line: you see the per-head price, the service fee and any charge for stations or linen before you confirm, which is why clients searching for the best vegan catering Dubai offers tend to compare us on clarity, not just flavour.

replace_in_block.block_on_your_page: A Taste of Our Vegan Catering
replace_in_block.new_heading: Why choose myCHEF for vegan catering?
new_paragraphs: MyCHEF was founded by a chef trained in some of Europe's most demanding kitchens, on one idea: you own the evening, we carry the work. MyCHEF is implementing a 12-stage partner verification framework , and what runs today is the documentation half of it: we check the partner's trade licence and permitted activities, the relevant Dubai Municipality approvals, food-safety documentation and insurance before a booking is confirmed, record expiry dates and ask for renewed documents when they fall due. We are honest about it, too: no system removes every risk, so we match each event to the partner and chef well suited to it. For plant-based and Mediterranean menus that is often Marco Rossi , with 15+ years, raised in Tuscany and trained in Rome and Milan, happiest working the grill and building antipasti and mezze that turn vegetables into the main event. Alongside vegan catering we have delivered villa weddings, yacht celebrations and corporate galas in Dubai. Client reviews are published only as events are delivered — real feedback, not invented.

replace_in_block.new_heading: What's on a vegan catering menu?
new_paragraphs: A vegan menu with myCHEF is built around a few hero mains and a spread of smaller plates, so every guest finds something they love instead of settling. Menus lean on Asian, Mediterranean and Indian cooking — mezze and grilled vegetables, dal, biryani and curries, dumplings and noodle bowls, plus grazing boards of marinated vegetables, dips and house breads. Plant-based mains run from jackfruit and mushroom centrepieces to stuffed aubergine and cauliflower steaks, and vegan desserts close the meal without dairy or eggs. Marco's Mediterranean background brings antipasti, wood-grilled produce and rustic sharing dishes to the table when you want that style. Portions are planned per head so the spread still looks generous for the last guest. Share your favourites and any no-go ingredients, and you get two or three menu directions at different price points, from a relaxed home spread to a plated tasting menu.

add_block.new_heading: Vegan catering for weddings, corporate events and parties
new_paragraphs: Vegan catering for events across Dubai suits almost any occasion, and the format shifts with the room. For weddings your chef plates multi-course plant-based menus that hold their own beside any banquet, dressed to your palette. Corporate vegan catering fits launches, board lunches and conferences, where clean logistics and a menu every guest can eat matter as much as the food. For a birthday or vegan party catering at home, we lean into grazing boards, sharing plates and showpiece mains guests photograph first. The same service covers baby showers, engagements, Ramadan majlis evenings and milestone dinners. Because the menu is fully plant-based, it also solves the mixed-diet table: nobody is handed a token side while the rest of the table eats properly. Tell us the occasion and the venue and we shape the volume, the courses and the flavours to match — a gala wants presence, a villa dinner wants restraint.

add_block.new_heading: The vegan catering menu, course by course
new_paragraphs: This is the working list our plant-based menus are drawn from, in serving order. You do not take all of it. A buffet usually runs one soup, three to five salads, four to six starters, one dal, one or two vegetable mains, a rice, two breads, an accompaniment and a dessert; the rest sits in reserve as choices. Dishes that need dairy stay on the vegetarian list and are not quietly relabelled, because a vegan guest and an Indian-vegetarian guest are asking two different questions.
Welcome drinks
One drink is normally included, chosen from four or five. The plant-based side of this list is short and honest, because most of the classic Indian welcome drinks are dairy.
Classic Lemonade: fresh lemon and mint over ice, the default in Dubai heat.
Fresh Juices and Smoothies: seasonal fruit blended to order at the drinks table.
Govindas Thandai: the spiced almond-and-saffron cooler, made on plant milk.
Chaas: the spiced buttermilk-style cooler with cumin and coriander, built on plant milk for a vegan menu.
Kesariya Lassi, Mango Lassi and Rabri Faluda are dairy drinks and stay on the vegetarian list.
Cold mezze — the naturally plant-based opening
Six to ten items, and the whole tier is vegan without adjusting anything. Built as a grazing table it becomes the whole first hour of a reception.
Hommos: chickpea and tahini dip, olive oil and lemon.
Moutabal: smoked aubergine whipped smooth with tahini.
Baba Ghanouj: chopped smoked aubergine with tomato, onion and pomegranate molasses.
Muhammara: red pepper and walnut, sharpened with pomegranate.
Fattoush: sumac-dressed salad with toasted Arabic bread through it.
Tabbouleh: parsley, mint, tomato and cracked wheat, lemon-heavy.
Stuffed Vine Leaves: rice, herbs and lemon, rolled and served cold.
Eggplant Salad: roasted aubergine dressed plainly, the quiet one on the tier.
Crudité: cucumber, tomato, radish and carrot cut for the dips.
Olives, Arabic Bread and Kaak Sticks: what the rest of the tier is eaten with.
Salads
Three to five on a buffet. The grain and pulse salads carry a plant-based table further than leaves do, so we usually take at least one of each.
Quinoa Salad: quinoa with herbs and a citrus dressing.
Kale Salad with Walnuts, Mango & Strawberry: the one guests photograph.
Baby Spinach Salad with Pomegranate: light, sharp, good beside heavier mains.
Beetroot Salad with Sweet Corn: earthy and sweet, holds well on a buffet.
Lentil Salad: cooked lentils, onion, herbs and vinaigrette.
Three Beans Salad: mixed beans dressed cold, a filling plant-based line.
Rajma Salad: kidney beans with onion, tomato and lemon.
Aloo Chana Chat Salad: potato and chickpea in chaat spicing.
Indian Summer Salad: crisp vegetables with a light spiced dressing.
Oriental Salad: shredded vegetables with a soy and sesame dressing.
Moong Sprout Salad: sprouted moong with onion, tomato and lemon.
Watermelon and Avocado Salad: the hot-weather salad, served late in the meal.
Thai Spinach Nut Salad: spinach, peanuts and a lime-chilli dressing.
Soup
One on a buffet, and it earns its place at winter and evening events more than at a summer lunch.
Coriander Lemon: clear, sharp and light.
Clear Vegetable: the plainest option, and the safest on a mixed table.
Sweet Corn: thick, mild, the one children eat.
Broccoli: blended green soup finished without dairy.
Cream of Tomato: finished with plant cream instead of dairy.
Canapés, cold and pass-around
Six to eight varieties for a standing reception, passed while guests are still arriving.
Canapé Chaat in Taco Cups: chaat spicing in a crisp cup, eaten in one bite.
Hummus Beetroot in Tartlet: hummus and beetroot in a short pastry case.
Mini Hummus & Roasted Pepper Phyllo Bites: crisp phyllo, hummus, roasted pepper.
Spinach Artichoke Stuffed Mushrooms: baked mushroom caps, served warm.
Vine Leaves with Plant Tzatziki in Shooters: a rolled vine leaf standing in a shot glass.
Cucumber Mint Gazpacho in Shots: cold soup as a pass-around.
Crisp Vegetable Tarts: thin pastry with roasted vegetables.
Bite-Sized Vegetable Skewers: grilled vegetables on a stick, no cutlery needed.
Hot starters — the Indian tray
Four to six, and this is where a plant-based buffet earns its reputation. Almost the whole tray is vegan as written, which is unusual for a hot-starter course.
Hara Bara Kebab: spinach, pea and potato patty, fried green.
Vegetable Pakora: mixed vegetables in gram-flour batter.
Vegetable Shami Kabab: soft spiced patty bound with pulses.
Green Pea Kachori: crisp pastry with a spiced pea filling.
Vegetable Kathi Roll: paratha rolled around spiced vegetables.
Vegetable Samosa: the standard triangle, potato and pea.
Punjabi Samosa: larger, heavier spicing, coarser potato.
Aloo Tikki: griddled potato cake, crisp outside.
Aloo Bonda: potato ball in gram-flour batter.
Vada Pav with Green Chutney: the Mumbai potato bun, served with chutney.
Dry Gobi Manchurian: fried cauliflower tossed in an Indo-Chinese sauce.
Masala Vada: crumbly chana-dal fritter.
Dal Vada: lentil fritter, crisp at the edges.
Bajri Vada: millet-flour fritter, a Gujarati line.
Kothimbir Vadi: steamed then fried coriander and gram-flour squares.
Dhokla: steamed gram-flour sponge, tempered with mustard seed.
Khandvi: rolled gram-flour ribbons, soft and delicate.
Patra: colocasia leaves rolled with spiced paste, steamed and sliced.
Handvo: savoury baked lentil and rice cake.
Fafda and Papdi Gathiya: crisp gram-flour snacks from the Gujarati tray.
Sev Khamni: crumbled chana with sev over the top.
Cut Mirchi: split chillies in batter, for the guests who ask for heat.
Idli with Chutney: steamed rice cakes, served with coconut or tomato chutney.
Hot starters — Arabic and international
Four to six alongside the Indian tray, which stops the hot course reading as one cuisine.
Mini Falafel Wrap: falafel, salad and tahina in a small wrap.
Spinach Fatayer: baked spinach and lemon pastry triangles.
Vegetable Spring Roll: crisp rolls with a shredded vegetable filling.
Crispy Baked Zucchini Fries: baked, not deep-fried, courgette sticks.
Vegetable Tempura: light batter, fried to order at a station or plated.
Vegetable Fajita Wrap with Guacamole: warm peppers and onion, guacamole through it.
Vegetable Puffs: flaky pastry around a spiced vegetable filling.
Cheese Sambousek, Grilled Halloumi with Cherry Tomato and the mini Margherita pizzas belong to the vegetarian tray, not this one.
The chaat counter
Sold as its own counter, not a garnish on the buffet, and running four to six chaats assembled in front of the guest.
Pani Puri and Golgappa: crisp shells filled to order with spiced water.
Sev Puri: flat puri, potato, chutneys and a heap of sev.
Bhel Puri: puffed rice tossed with chutney and onion at the counter.
Papdi Chaat: crisp discs layered with potato, chickpea and chutneys.
Samosa Chaat: a samosa broken open and dressed with chole and chutney.
Raj Kachori: the large filled kachori, the showpiece of the counter.
Aloo Chat: spiced potato, sharp and quick to serve.
Pav Bhaji: mashed spiced vegetables with griddled buns.
The yoghurt chaats — Dahi Puri, Dahi Bhalla, Dahi Chana Chat — run on the vegetarian counter.
Indian mains — the dal line
One dal per menu, named on the quote rather than left as "a dal". It is the line that decides whether the buffet tastes home-cooked.
Dal Tadka: yellow dal finished with a hot tempering of cumin and chilli.
Daal Palak: lentils cooked down with spinach.
Gujarati Daal: the sweet-sour version, lighter than a Punjabi dal.
Rasawala Moong: thin, brothy moong dal.
Paanch Kathol: five pulses cooked together, a Gujarati staple.
Kadhai Daal: dal finished in the kadhai with peppers and tomato.
Dal Khichdi: dal and rice cooked together, soft and comforting.
Dal Baati Churma: the Rajasthani version, dal with baked baati and sweet churma.
Dal Makhani takes butter and cream, so it sits on the vegetarian menu.
Indian mains — the vegetable line
One or two vegetable lines per menu. The regional ones are what stop an Indian buffet reading as generic.
Chole: chickpeas in a dark, tangy Punjabi masala.
Aloo Gobhi: potato and cauliflower, dry-cooked with turmeric and cumin.
Bhindi Masala: okra cooked with onion and tomato.
Bharela Bhinda: okra stuffed whole with a spiced gram-flour paste.
Gatte ki Sabji: Rajasthani gram-flour dumplings in a spiced gravy.
Ker Sangri: the Rajasthani desert-bean and berry dish, sharp and dry.
Kaju Karela: bitter gourd cooked with cashew to balance it.
Tindora Capsicum: ivy gourd and pepper, stir-cooked dry.
Cauliflower & Nuts: roasted cauliflower with toasted nuts through it.
Mixed Vegetables: the plain seasonal line every buffet needs.
Vegetable Manchurian: Indo-Chinese vegetable balls in a dark sauce.
Baby Corn Manchurian: the same treatment, crisper and lighter.
Sarson da Saag with Makke di Roti: mustard greens with corn flatbread, a winter menu.
Chole Bhature: chickpeas with puffed fried bread, a brunch-weight dish.
Continental and pan-Asian mains
Three or four on a plant-based buffet. This is the course that carries a mixed-nationality guest list, because not every table wants an Indian main.
Red Lentil & Sweet Potato Curry with Spinach: thick, mild and filling.
Baked Bell Pepper filled with Quinoa Stuffing: a plated-looking centrepiece that holds on a buffet.
Vegetable Ratatouille: slow-cooked summer vegetables in tomato.
Italian Roasted Vegetables with Herbs: tray-roasted, dressed with olive oil.
Grilled Mixed Vegetables with Pesto: charred vegetables under a dairy-free pesto.
Spinach with Chickpeas, Lemon and Garlic: the simplest dish on the list and often the most eaten.
Maple Glazed Root Vegetables: sweet, glossy, a festive-table regular.
Lemon Garlic Roasted Broccoli and Carrots: bright and plain, it sits beside anything.
Cauliflower Provencal: cauliflower with tomato, olive and herbs.
Vegetable Szechuan: hot and sour, the sharpest thing on the buffet.
Thai Coconut Chickpeas Curry: coconut milk, lemongrass and chickpea.
Thai Vegetable Curry: red or green, built on coconut milk.
Spicy Tofu with Creamy Coconut Sauce: tofu treated as a main, not a substitute.
Red Tofu Curry with Mushrooms: deeper and darker than the Thai curries.
Mushroom Tofu Stroganoff: the creamy option, made on plant cream.
Lentil Shepherd's Pie: lentil base under mashed potato, a real centrepiece.
Roasted Vegetable Couscous: couscous with roasted vegetables through it.
Quinoa Tabbouleh: the Levantine salad rebuilt on quinoa, served warm or cold.
Risotto: mushroom, beetroot or butternut, finished without dairy.
Pasta and noodles
One or two lines, and they do more work than their position suggests — this is the course teenagers and fussy eaters go to.
Spaghetti in Creamy Tomato Sauce with Pesto: rich without cream.
Creamy Pepper and Tomato Pasta: roasted peppers blended into the sauce.
Penne Pomodoro: plain tomato and basil, the safe line.
Penne Arrabiata: chilli and garlic, served without the parmesan.
Fusilli with Vegetables: spirals holding a chunky vegetable sauce.
Macaroni al Pesto: short pasta under a dairy-free pesto.
Hakka Tofu Noodles: stir-fried noodles with tofu and shredded vegetables.
Teriyaki Mushroom & Broccoli Noodles: sweet-salty and dark.
Vegetable Chow Mein: the familiar one, quick to serve in volume.
Hong Kong Noodles: crisp-fried noodles under a vegetable sauce.
Triple Schezwan Rice: rice, noodles and sauce together, hot and loud.
Rice and biryani
One named rice line per menu. Naming the region is the difference between a rice dish and a rice line item.
Handi Hyderabadi Biryani: sealed-pot biryani, the one to order if you order one.
Vegetable Biryani: layered rice and spiced vegetables.
Jeera Rice: basmati with cumin, made to sit under a dal.
Green Peas Pulao: light pulao, good beside a heavy main.
Lemon Rice: south Indian, sharp with mustard seed and curry leaf.
Steamed Basmati Rice: the plain default, on every table.
Moong Daal Khichdi: soft rice and moong, gentle food.
Vagharela Khichdi: khichdi finished with a Gujarati tempering.
Fada Khichdi: cracked-wheat khichdi, nuttier than the rice version.
Breads
Two on a standard menu and three on the top tier, cooked through the service, not stacked in advance.
Naan: plain or masala, on the vegan build made without butter or yoghurt.
Lachha Paratha: layered and flaky, torn not cut.
Missi Roti: gram-flour roti with onion and spice worked in.
Kulcha: soft leavened bread from the tandoor.
Chapati and Rotli: the everyday thin flatbreads.
Whole Wheat Poori: puffed and fried, a festive bread.
Bhakri: thick rustic flatbread, sturdy under a wet curry.
Bajari Rotla: millet flatbread, dense and naturally gluten-free.
Methi Thepla: fenugreek-flecked Gujarati flatbread.
Makke di Roti: corn flatbread, the partner to sarson da saag.
Potatoes, sides and accompaniments
One or two potato lines and the small dishes that make a buffet feel finished, not assembled.
Roasted Potato with Herbs: the default side, roasted in oil not butter.
Roasted Hasselback Potatoes: fanned and crisped, the festive-table version.
Mexican Potato: paprika and chilli spicing.
Parsley Potato: boiled and tossed with parsley and oil.
Lyonnaise Potato: sliced potato cooked down with onion.
Spicy Potato: dry-spiced and hot.
Steamed Potato: plain, for the guests keeping it light.
Whole Baked Potato: baked in the skin, split at service.
Baked French Onion Potato: sweet onion baked through the potato.
Potato Wedges: the one that disappears first at a party.
Grilled Vegetables: charred seasonal vegetables, dressed with oil and lemon.
Papad: crisp lentil wafers, plain or masala.
Mint Chutney: fresh and green, the sharp one.
Sweet Tamarind Chutney: dark and sticky, the counterweight.
Spicy Green Chutney: chilli-forward, for the chaat counter.
Mixed Pickle: oily, salty, in small quantity.
Kachumber: chopped cucumber, tomato and onion with lemon.
Boondi, cucumber and mixed vegetable raita are yoghurt-based and go on the vegetarian side.
Live stations
An intimate event takes one or two, a wedding three to five, and each station is quoted with its contents, not as a name on a list:
Chaat Station: pani puri, sev puri and samosa chat assembled in front of the guest.
Falafel Station: Arabic bread, tomato, parsley, Arabic pickles, tahina sauce.
Saj Station: zaatar on the vegan build; labneh and cheese saj on the vegetarian one.
Dosa Counter and Tawa Counter: dosa to order, or a tawa working through the vegetable and paratha list.
Indo-Chinese Counter: Manchurian, Szechuan and Hakka noodles cooked to order.
Pasta Station: tagliatelle, farfalle and penne with pesto or tomato sauce.
Asian Station: vegetable tempura and spring rolls fried to order.
Mexican Station: vegetable fajita, guacamole, salsa, red beans; quesadilla on the vegetarian build.
Tandoor and Grill Station: vegetable and soya chaap skewers, with paneer tikka on the vegetarian build — this is the Jain BBQ format too, cooked with no onion and no garlic.
Sandwich and Kathi Roll Station: tofu, falafel or grilled-vegetable fillings.
Gola and Kulfi Falooda Station: the sweet end of a summer event; kulfi is dairy, gola is not.

Three of those stations are decided by your address, not by your menu. Start with the saj, which places almost anywhere: an electric saj dome needs no fuel approval and runs in a villa kitchen, on a villa terrace or inside an apartment on a socket with headroom, while a gas saj stays outdoors at ground level at a villa, because the UAE Fire Code keeps LPG cylinders out of indoor spaces (11-2.2.6) and off roofs and terraces (Table 11.1). Neither version goes aboard a yacht — D-Marin Art. 53.1(a) allows only the vessel's own installed gas supply, and Dubai Harbour section 7.4 bans operating gas cylinders on marina premises — so the zaatar and manakish breads bake in the licensed kitchen and the live element becomes a fill-and-roll counter on deck.

The tandoor and grill station is a villa and garden setup, confirmed for the specific plot when you book, and it stays outdoors: Dubai Municipality's barbecue guidance says not to light coal in an enclosed space or indoors. In an apartment it does not run at all, because Emaar's vertical-community rules prohibit barbecues, grills or any cooking equipment of any kind on balconies and terraces regardless of fuel. There the soya chaap and vegetable skewers are charred in the partner kitchen and finished on an induction counter in front of guests. Frying to order — tempura, spring rolls, poori, luqaimat — wants an outdoor position at a villa and is refused inside a tower, where a grease-heavy appliance would need a Type I extraction hood and wet-chemical suppression that no residential kitchen has; those items are fried short in the licensed kitchen and crisped to order on site. For a rooftop or a desert site, myCHEF confirms the setup with the building management or the landowner before quoting.
The paneer line — vegetarian, not vegan

Plenty of tables are mixed, so the vegetarian list runs in parallel, not as a substitution note. Paneer is its own named line on every Indian menu, and it is dairy, so it does not cross onto the vegan build.
Paneer Kadai: paneer with peppers and onion in a dry kadai masala.
Paneer Butter Masala: the sweet, rich tomato gravy.
Palak Paneer: paneer in cooked-down spinach.
Paneer Tikka Masala: grilled paneer finished in gravy.
Muttar Paneer: peas and paneer, mild and familiar.
Methi Malai Muttar: fenugreek, cream and peas.
Paneer Malai Tikka: marinated and grilled, served dry.
Baked Paneer: baked, not fried, so it sits lighter on the plate.
Soya Chaap Makhani: soya chaap in a makhani gravy, the paneer alternative.
The Jain module
The Jain menu is re-engineered, not stripped — no onion, no garlic, no root vegetables, and the strong versions name what replaced what.
Jain Pav Bhaji: built on raw banana in place of potato.
Gatta Curry: besan dumplings standing in for a root sabzi.
Jain Dal Makhani: the makhani dal without onion or garlic.
Jain Mix Veg: seasonal vegetables, no roots.
Jain Tawa Paneer: griddled paneer, Jain spicing.
Jain Bhindi Masala: okra cooked without onion or garlic.
Jain Kofta Curry: vegetable koftas in a Jain gravy.
Jain Chole Bhature: chickpeas and fried bread, re-spiced.
Jain Pulao: rice with vegetables and whole spice.
Jain Khichdi: plain rice and moong, gentle and quick.
Jain Stuffed Paratha: filled without potato or onion.
Dhokla: in the Khaman, Edada and Sandwich versions.
Khandvi: rolled gram-flour ribbons.
Handvo: baked savoury lentil and rice cake.
Patra: steamed spiced leaf rolls, sliced and tempered.
Sev Khamni: crumbled chana under sev.
Ultimate Jain Thali: mixed dal, a paneer curry, two seasonal vegetable curries, flavoured or plain rice, and fresh rotis or parathas as one composed plate.
Desserts, cakes and the sweet table
The vegan sweet table opens with a dairy-free line instead of apologising at the end. Eggless is listed separately from vegan on purpose, because the two buyers are asking different questions.
Dairy-Free Chocolate Mousse: set on plant cream, the default vegan dessert.
Awamat with Date Syrup: fried dough soaked in date syrup, not honey.
Luqaimat: crisp outside, soft inside, served warm.
Apple Crumble: baked with a dairy-free crumble topping.
Fruit Canapés and Fresh Fruit Platter: cut fruit as a dessert course, not a garnish.
Raw Plant-Based Desserts: nut and date bases, set in the fridge, not baked.
Eggless Cakes: made without egg, which is not the same as vegan — we list the two apart.
Indian mithai is dairy and belongs to the vegetarian menu, not this one:
Gulab Jamun: fried milk-solid balls in sugar syrup.
Ras Mallai: soft cheese discs in sweetened milk.
Rasgulla: syrup-soaked cheese balls, lighter than gulab jamun.
Jalebi with Rabri: crisp spirals under thickened milk.
Gajar Halwa: slow-cooked carrot with milk and ghee.
Rice Kheer: rice pudding with cardamom.
Kulfi Falooda: dense frozen milk dessert with vermicelli.
If you have been shortlisting vegan dessert places in Dubai for a birthday cake or a dessert bar, this is the same idea brought to your venue instead of a counter.
Bakery, high tea and the cafe-style questions

A vegan cafe in Dubai and a vegan caterer are answering different briefs: one seats you, the other travels. Where the two meet is high tea and morning catering, and there the honest answer is that laminated pastry is a specialist job. A dairy-free croissant, or a vegan croissant in Dubai made properly with plant-based lamination, depends on whether the assigned culinary partner has that bakery capability, so we confirm it for your booking before we put it on your menu. The same goes for a fully vegetarian preparation environment, which some partners run and others do not: we check it against the partner assigned to your event.
Festive and seasonal menus

Seasonal menus come out of the same list, not a separate one. A vegan Christmas dinner in Dubai builds around maple glazed root vegetables, roasted hasselback potatoes and a centrepiece — baked bell pepper with quinoa stuffing, or lentil shepherd's pie — finished with apple crumble. Diwali and Navratri menus lean on the chaat counter, the mithai list and a Handi Hyderabadi Biryani; Ramadan majlis evenings take the mezze tier, luqaimat and a saj station.
Dietary notes, stated plainly

Gluten-free, nut-conscious and other dietary menu options may be available on request, subject to confirmation by the assigned culinary partner. Partner kitchens may handle allergens, and cross-contact cannot be completely excluded unless dedicated controls have been specifically confirmed for the booking. Guests with allergies must provide full details before confirming their event. Jain and sattvic requirements are handled the same way: named on the brief, confirmed with the partner, and written into the menu before it is signed off.
Formats, minimums and what each one costs

Volume formats start at 10 guests, buffets at 20, and the minimum order value is AED 900. A working or office lunch runs from AED 90 per person, a standard event buffet from AED 120, and a premium buffet, canapé or live-station build from AED 150. Staffed service — a chef cooking and serving on site, plated — is the AED 700 to 950 band, and the difference you are paying for is labour and courses, not better vegetables. Is Dubai vegan friendly on the supply side? Yes: plant-based produce, tofu, plant milks and specialist ingredients are all here year-round, which is why a fully vegan menu costs no more than a mixed one at the same format.

add_block.new_heading: Which dietary needs can a vegan menu cover?
new_paragraphs: A vegan menu already removes meat, dairy, eggs and honey, and we layer further restrictions on top without losing flavour. Nut-free, gluten-free, soy-free and low-oil versions are all doable, and we cross-check every ingredient and cooking surface when an allergy is serious instead of a preference. For halal households the plant-based menu is inherently suitable, and we keep alcohol out of the cooking on request. We label each dish on the final menu so a guest with coeliac disease or a nut allergy can see what is in front of them and raise anything with us before the event rather than guessing at the table. If your table mixes vegan, vegetarian and omnivore guests, we can run a plant-based core with a couple of add-on dishes so one kitchen still serves every guest. Flag the needs when you share your date, and the chef designs around them from the first draft — not as an afterthought bolted on at the venue.

new_paragraphs: How much does vegan catering cost in Dubai?

Vegan catering starts from about AED 700 per person, with the final figure set by guest count, menu and how much service you want. Buffet and drop-off formats cost less per head than plated service with staff, and larger events move onto catering packages from AED 1,200.
What is included in vegan catering?

Menu design and tasting, a vetted chef cooking on site, service staff where needed, the plating and the full cleanup are all included. You see the per-head price, service and any rentals itemised before you confirm.
How do I hire a vegan caterer in Dubai?
Share your date, guest count and venue and we match a vetted chef and send an itemised proposal, usually within one business day. Approve it and pay to confirm the date.
Is the food completely plant-based and dairy-free?

Yes. Every dish is fully plant-based with no meat, dairy, eggs or honey. We flag any shared-kitchen or allergen concerns on the menu before the event and can build nut-free or gluten-free vegan menus on request.
Can you cater vegan food for weddings and corporate events?
Yes. We build vegan menus for weddings, corporate launches, parties and private celebrations across Dubai, scaling from a dozen guests to several hundred with plated, buffet or live-station service.
Do you offer vegan catering packages?
Yes. Catering packages start at AED 1,200 and step up through AED 2,400, 3,600, 4,500 and 5,500 as guest numbers and courses grow, which keeps larger vegan events predictable.
Is Dubai vegan friendly?

Yes, and more so every year. Dedicated plant-based restaurants and cafes now trade across the city, most restaurant menus mark vegetarian dishes and a growing number mark vegan ones, and supermarkets carry plant milks, tofu, tempeh and vegan cheese as standard stock. Arabic cooking helps too: mezze such as hummus, moutabel, tabbouleh, warak enab and falafel is plant-based before anyone adapts it. For catering the practical answer is that a fully vegan menu needs no imported workaround here — the produce, the ingredients and the chefs who cook with them are all local.
Which areas of Dubai do you cover?
We cover homes, villas, offices and venues across Dubai, from Palm Jumeirah and Emirates Hills to Business Bay, Dubai Marina, Downtown and the beach clubs.
For vegan catering, the chefs and partner kitchens handling your booking operate to Dubai Municipality food-safety requirements .
